title: Traveling vine scarf
subtitle: A diagonal lace vine that moves across the fabric on every right-side row.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat in a traveling vine lace pattern on 4 mm needles with DK-weight yarn, finishing at 18 cm wide by 175 cm long after blocking. The vine motif uses paired yarn-overs and decreases to shift a column of eyelets diagonally across the width, creating an S-curve effect when viewed across the full length.
sourceNotes: Traveling vine and diagonal lace patterns appear in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive. Barbara Walker's A Treasury of Knitting Patterns (1968) documents multiple travelling-stitch vine variants, cited as a modern compilation of historical techniques.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat from one short end to the other in a traveling vine lace pattern on 4 mm needles. It finishes at 18 cm wide and 175 cm long after blocking. The vine effect comes from moving a yarn-over and k2tog pair one stitch to the right on every RS row. The eyelet column traces a slow diagonal across the width over eight rows, then returns via the mirror repeat.

Flat construction keeps the vine pattern easy to read from a chart, row by row. WS rows are simply purled across. DK yarn on 4 mm needles gives a lace fabric open enough to see the vine clearly. The finished scarf needs about 360 m (around 130 g) and drapes easily around the neck.
What you need

items.name: DK-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Any DK-weight yarn. A smooth plied yarn shows the vine diagonal most clearly.

items.name: 4 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 8 / US 6)
items.qty: 1 pair or 1 circular 60 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 sts x 28 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. In traveling vine lace the gauge is approximately 20 sts per 10 cm because the eyelets open the fabric slightly. Swatch the 10-stitch repeat and block before measuring. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by approximately 1 cm at this stitch count. Row gauge drift across the full 455 rows changes the finished length by up to 15 cm.
Stitches used
K (knit), P (purl), YO (yarn over, UK: yfwd between knit stitches), K2tog (right-leaning decrease). See the leaf lace scarf for full descriptions.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 40 stitches on the needle. The 40 stitches give you 4 repeats of 10 stitches across the body. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 4 mm needles (circumference approximately 12.6 mm) and 40 stitches: (12.6 x 40) / 10 + 15 = 50.4 + 15 = about 65 cm. Leave a tail of at least 65 cm.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 40 stitches on the needle.
Body

Work a 1-stitch garter selvedge at each edge on every row. The 38 centre stitches work the vine pattern across 3 full repeats plus 8 extra stitches (follow the chart for the partial repeats at each edge). The vine shifts one position to the right each RS row through rows 1, 3, 5, 7, then mirrors back left through rows 9, 11, 13, 15 of a 16-row full pattern.
Row 1 (RS): K1 selvedge, [K2, YO, K2, K2tog, K2] 4 times, K1 selvedge. (40 sts)
Row 2 and all WS rows: K1 selvedge, P38, K1 selvedge. (40 sts)
Row 3 (RS): K1 selvedge, [K2, K1, YO, K2, K2tog, K1] adjusted repeat -- follow the chart, shifting the YO one position right of row 1. (40 sts)

Continue following the chart, shifting the YO and K2tog pair one position right on each RS row for 4 rows, then shifting left for 4 rows, completing the vine cycle. Repeat the full 16-row vine cycle until the scarf measures 175 cm. At the halfway mark (approximately row 228, around 87 cm), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 228 you should have 40 stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a suspended bind-off on a right-side row for a loose, open edge that pins well during blocking.
Common faults

Vine not shifting consistently. The vine moves by placing the YO one stitch further right on each RS row. If the vine appears to jump or double back unexpectedly, check whether the YO position matches the chart for that row number.
Stitch count rising. Each YO must be paired with exactly one K2tog in the same row. If the count rises after a RS row, a K2tog was missed. Check by counting pairs as you work each repeat.

Vine shape barely visible before blocking. DK lace compresses during knitting. The diagonal eyelet column will be much more pronounced after blocking. Wet block fully before judging the pattern success.
Finishing
Weave in both tails along the selvedge edge and trim.
Wet blocking
is required to open the vine motif. Soak in cool water for 20 minutes, press out gently, roll in a towel, and pin flat to 18 x 175 cm on the blocking mat. Leave fully flat until dry.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry, easing gently to the stated dimensions.
What to try next

The leaf lace scarf uses a similar yarn-over and decrease vocabulary but produces a static repeating motif rather than a traveling one. The feather and fan scarf uses yarn-overs in groups with multiple decreases and increases to make a wider wave pattern.
